Four modes: (1) **Concealment mode** — hatred operates within while the person presents a false exterior (Pro 10:18: "the one who conceals hatred has lying lips"; Pro 26:24: "whoever hates disguises himself with his lips and harbours deceit in his heart"). (2) **Accumulation mode** — hatred intensifies when fed by new provocations (Gen 37:5, 8: "they hated him even more"). (3) **Settlement mode** — sa.tam: the hatred settles into a plan (Gen 27:41: Esau says internally "then I will kill my brother Jacob"). (4) **Expression mode** — hatred breaks through into visible behaviour when restraint fails (Eze 35:11: "the anger and envy that you showed because of your hatred against them").

Four modes: (1) **Inner speech mode** — the contempt is articulated privately (Psa 10:13: "say in his heart, 'You will not call to account'"). (2) **Behavioural mode** — the inner verdict produces action in accordance with it (Num 15:31: "because he has despised the word...he has broken his commandment"). (3) **Speech-act mode** — ne.a.tsah: blasphemous contempt expressed outward in speech (Neh 9:18, 9:26, Eze 35:12). (4) **Contagion mode** — biz.za.von: contempt spreading from one person's act through a community (Est 1:18).

Three modes: (1) **Righteous abhorrence** — the person's visceral recoil from evil, falsehood, and what violates moral truth, aligned with God's own (Psa 119:163). (2) **Inverted abhorrence** — the same capacity directed against justice and truth (Amo 5:10, Mic 3:9). (3) **Divine sustained abhorrence** — God's settled inner revulsion toward those who have persistently corrupted themselves (Psa 106:40, Amo 6:8).

Three modes: (1) **Character-quality mode** — cruelty as the persistent inner quality characterising the person (Pro 12:10: "the mercy of the wicked is cruel"). (2) **Oppressor-disposition mode** — ruthlessness as the inner character of those who do not set God before themselves (Psa 54:3). (3) **Terror-as-instrument mode** — the ruthless nations deployed by God as instruments of judgment (Eze 28:7, 30:11, 32:12 — "the most ruthless of nations").

Four modes: (1) **Personal acute mode** — ne.a.tsah: the overwhelming shame-experience in a moment of crisis (2Ki 19:3). (2) **Personal chronic mode** — cher.pah (individual): the sustained inner-social condition of the person publicly designated as shameful (Psa 69:7). (3) **Corporate-covenantal mode** — cher.pah (communal): reproach as the condition of a whole people among the nations (Eze 5:14). (4) **Dignity-violation mode** — hubrizō: reproach as the experience of having one's dignity actively stripped (1Th 2:2).

Three modes: (1) **Legal/judicial mode** — antidikos: the adversary in a legal dispute generating urgency (Mat 5:25, Luk 12:58, 18:3). (2) **Covenantal-advocacy mode** — a.yav, ya.riv: God as adversary on behalf of the covenant person, generating appeal and confidence (Exo 23:22, Psa 35:1, Isa 49:25). (3) **Cosmic-spiritual mode** — antidikos: the devil as the adversary who prowls seeking to devour (1Pe 5:8), generating sober watchfulness.

One mode with three distinctive features: **Soul-level pleasure in destruction** as the primary mode (Eze 25:6: "rejoiced with all the malice within your soul"); **purposive destruction** driving actively toward harm (Eze 25:15: "to destroy in never-ending enmity"); **contempt-compound** where joy and contempt are simultaneous and inseparable (Eze 36:5: "wholehearted joy and utter contempt").

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** God's righteousness operates in the human context through: (1) appeal — the psalmist appeals to God's righteousness as the ground for deliverance (A1-004); (2) exposure — it exposes human unrighteousness by contrast (A1-006; Act 24:25: Felix alarmed); (3) proclamation — it must be declared and testified to (A1-005); (4) covenant — as the ground of God's faithfulness toward his people (A1-003).

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Human righteousness operates through at least seven distinct inner modes: (1) governing state structuring the whole inner life; (2) orientation toward God (A2-014: walking with him, born of him); (3) orientation toward others (A2-012: flowing outward); (4) response — gladness, exultation, praise (3246-003); (5) pursuit — hungered for, actively sought (A2-006); (6) identity — worn, carried, defining characterisation (A2-009); (7) life path — recognisable trajectory (A2-017).

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** Uprightness operates through: (1) direction of speech — speaking what is right and true (Isa 33:15; Isa 45:19); (2) direction of the will — choosing the straight path (Pro 2:13–14); (3) orientation of the heart — uprightness of heart as inner state (1211-001); (4) recognition of what is right — enabling discernment of right paths (Pro 2:9).

**[C — Justification]** Operates: (1) as divine declaration — the verdict is passed and the person's standing changes (3194-001); (2) as received condition — received by faith (Gal 3:24; Tit 3:7); (3) as historical precedent extended — Abraham's case becomes the pattern for all believers (3410-001 cross-reference); (4) as inner transformation of self-understanding — the justified person can count themselves as one who stands rightly before God.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** Operates through: (1) the cry — the inner movement of the wronged person toward God in petition (944-001); (2) the commission — the inner acceptance of delegated authority to execute retribution (3250-001); (3) the relinquishment — the inner act of entrusting personal vengeance to God (6841-002); (4) the inner recognition of God's freedom from human claims (6841-004).

**[E — Condemnation]** Operates through: (1) the external verdict — judicial sentence directed at the person from outside (4846-001); (2) the inner weight — the person's experience of being under verdict; (3) the reflexive self-verdict — the inner being condemning itself (4848-001); (4) the release — the inner experience of freedom when the verdict is lifted (4846-002: Joh 8:10–11); (5) the moral testimony — the righteous generation condemning the unrighteous by comparison (4846-001: Ninevites).

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** The reckoning faculty operates through: (1) theological accounting — crediting faith as righteousness, counting status before God (3410-001: Rom 4); (2) ethical self-application — counting oneself dead to sin, alive to God (Rom 6:11); (3) comparative weighing — present suffering against future glory (Rom 8:18); (4) practical deliberation — reasoning about specific decisions (Mar 11:31; Joh 11:50); (5) moral valuation — deeming worthy or unworthy (1185-001: axioō); (6) devotional orientation — preparing oneself before God in prayer (6753-003: a.rakh).

**[G — Structural Opposites]** Wickedness operates through: (1) systemic injustice — oppressing the righteous through corrupt systems (M26-A2-010 cross-reference); (2) active opposition — plotting against and persecuting the righteous (M26-A2-016); (3) suppression of uprightness — demanding smooth things instead of what is right (Isa 30:10, VSG 1214-001); (4) occupation of righteous space — "wickedness is in the place of justice" (Ecc 3:16).

**[CLUSTER]** The cluster reveals that righteousness operates through a remarkably diverse set of inner modes: as appeal, as proclamation, as governing state, as pursuit, as identity, as orientation, as verdict, as self-application, as valuation, as entrusting. The diversity of modes is itself an analytical finding — righteousness does not operate in one way but engages the whole inner person through multiple faculties and in multiple directional vectors.

God is the primary subject across the verse landscape. The divine blessing (1299-001 — 89 verses, all God as subject), divine graciousness (2330-001 — 13 verses, all God), divine inner pleasure (795-001; 795-002 — ra.tsah with God as subject), divine grace (888-001 — charis, God as sovereign agent), divine goodwill (494-001 — eudokia, God as subject) collectively constitute the dominant subject-register. The human as subject (cha.nan generosity in 984-001; charizō human forgiveness in 5470-002; ba.rakh human blessing in 1299-002 and 1299-003) is the secondary and derivative register. God enacts; humans participate.

The human person is the primary subject — the one who is good, who evaluates as good, who does well. Tov group 542-001 has God as subject in the affirmation-form (1Ki 8:18; 2Ki 10:30 — God affirming human goodness) but the human is the agent of goodness being evaluated. Ya.tav group 632-002 (doing good) has the human as the moral actor. The goodness characteristic is more human-centred in subject than M39-A.

M46-A operates in two distinct modes. Mode 1: gradual satiation-produced dulling — the progressive process by which material abundance removes the edge of inner hunger, eventually producing a closed, fat heart. This is the sha.men verb pattern (Deu 32:15; Jer 5:28). Mode 2: false self-assessment anchoring — the inner act of grounding identity and security in material condition, producing blindness to actual inner state. This is the Rev 3:17 / Hos 12:8 pattern. Mode 1 is a process; Mode 2 is a stable (though false) inner orientation.

M46-B operates in two distinct modes. Mode 1: outward hardness — the eroded capacity for pity expressed in indifference to the suffering neighbor, rough treatment of petitioners, structural domination of the poor (Luk 16:19-21; 2Sa 12:4; Pro 18:23). Mode 2: inward insatiability — the inability of the inner person to receive what they have as sufficient, expressed in the never-satisfied eyes (Ecc 4:8), the inability to enjoy wealth held (Ecc 6:2), and the grief of material loss (Rev 18:15-19). Both modes are expressions of the same inner contraction but face in different directions.

M46-C operates in an evaluative-generative mode: the inner character of the person evaluates and generates the quality of the material life. The diligent inner person generates material sufficiency (Pro 13:4). The trusting inner person receives material enrichment as divine gift (Pro 28:25; Pro 10:22). The humble inner person receives riches as the reward of right orientation (Pro 22:4). M46-C's mode is the wisdom tradition's causal account: inner character as the generative principle of the material domain.

M46-D operates in three distinct modes. Mode 1: receptive openness — the inner posture of poverty of spirit (Mat 5:3) that receives from God without self-resistance. Mode 2: volitional release — the deliberate inner act of giving, refusing, or relinquishing material wealth in response to a higher valuation (Gen 14:23; Luk 19:8; 2Cor 8:9). Mode 3: learned settledness — the formed inner disposition of contentment that has been acquired through practice across circumstances (autarkēs, Phil 4:11). These three modes form a progression: openness to receive → willingness to release → settled independence from material circumstance.

M01-A operates in at least five distinct ways: (1) as moral restraint — substituting for external accountability where no human observer is present (Lev 19:14; Lev 25:43); (2) as epistemic foundation — ordering the cognitive life toward genuine knowledge (Pro 1:7; Pro 9:10; Psa 111:10); (3) as relational posture — positioning the person for covenant intimacy with God (Psa 25:14; Psa 103:11-13); (4) as identity marker — defining who the person is within a covenant community (Job 1:1; 1Ki 18:3; Neh 7:2); (5) as moral compass — redirecting the will away from evil and toward wisdom's path (Pro 8:13: "fear of God is the inner hatred of evil"; Pro 16:6; Pro 14:27).

M01-B operates as: (1) a will-governing impulse — driving flight, deception, or submission in response to threat (Gen 32:7 anchor; Gen 3:10; 1Sa 17:24); (2) a social moderator — shaping what is said and done in public through fear of crowd opinion (Mat 21:26 anchor; Joh 7:13; Gal 2:12); (3) an awe-register — producing worship-adjacent responses to divine or miraculous power (Mar 4:41 anchor; Act 2:43).

M01-C operates as: (1) a divine weapon — actively deployed by God to paralyse enemy resistance (Exo 23:27 anchor); (2) an encircling force — surrounding and pursuing the wicked with no escape (Job 18:11 anchor); (3) a quality projected by powerful entities that radiates outward (Hab 1:7 anchor; Song 6:4); (4) an instrument of imperial domination — the defining power of military empires over their subjects (Eze 32:23 anchor).

M01-D operates as: (1) a response to catastrophic news — collapsing confidence when the assumed order shatters (Psa 6:3 anchor; Gen 45:3); (2) a divine judicial instrument — God imposing inner collapse on rebels (Psa 2:5; Jer 49:37 anchor); (3) a bodily-manifest collapse — the inner shattering becoming visible on the body (Dan 5:6 anchor); (4) a rash agitation — the ba.hal register of impulsive urgency (Pro 28:22 anchor, D-VCG-05).

M01-E operates as: (1) involuntary theophanic trembling — the body's response to divine presence (Exo 19:16 anchor); (2) reverential somatic sobriety before God's word (Isa 66:2 anchor); (3) body-register of witnessed catastrophe (Eze 26:16 anchor); (4) military panic trembling — spreading contagiously through groups (1Sa 14:15 anchor); (5) visceral shuddering of flesh (Job 21:6 anchor); (6) NT somatic gravity in worship and ministry (Phili 2:12 anchor).

M01-F operates as: (1) pervasive daily anxiety — saturating ordinary activities (Eze 12:18 anchor); (2) anticipatory dread that materializes — the feared event arriving (Job 3:25 anchor); (3) covenantal curse-dread — chronic unrelenting anxiety as divine punishment (Deu 28:66 anchor); (4) dread of divine judgment — anticipatory fear of condemnation (Heb 10:27 anchor); (5) pastoral anxiety — protective forward-looking concern for others (2Cor 12:20 anchor).

M01-G operates as: (1) spirit-level constitutional deficiency — a settled inner posture of cowardly shrinking (2Ti 1:7 anchor); (2) will-suppression — paralysing faithful action (Mat 25:25; Luk 19:21); (3) apostasy-under-pressure — the social/political dimension of yielding to threat (Rev 21:8).

Across M01, fear operates in at least ten distinct modes: as moral restraint, epistemic foundation, relational posture, identity marker, moral compass (M01-A); as will-governing impulse, social moderator, and awe-register (M01-B); as weapon, encircling force, and projected quality (M01-C); as catastrophe-response, judicial instrument, and bodily collapse (M01-D); as theophanic trembling, reverential sobriety, and panic-contagion (M01-E); as chronic anxiety, anticipatory dread, and pastoral concern (M01-F); and as constitutional failure under pressure (M01-G). The volitional faculty is engaged across every mode.
As judicial verdict: wrath operates as a stored moral verdict that issues in binding consequences — Heb 3:11 (oath of exclusion); Deu 29:28 (exile).
As covenant discipline: burning anger operates as a directed disciplinary heat that drives historical consequences — Judg 2:14; Judg 3:8 (subjugation as consequence of kindled anger).
As action-driving impulse: incensed anger erupts into immediate outward action — Exo 32:19 (Moses smashing tablets); 2Ch 16:10 (Asa imprisoning the prophet).

As possessing force: rage fills and takes possession of the inner person, displacing other faculties — Est 3:5 (Haman filled with fury); Dan 3:19 (Nebuchadnezzar filled with fury, change visible on face).

As a state requiring restraint: anger is present but held in check — Psa 78:38 (God's compassion repeatedly restraining his warranted rage); Eph 4:26 (anger acknowledged as legitimate, requiring governance).
As sustained moral stance: indignation as a persistent inner posture maintained toward wrongdoing without necessarily erupting — Psa 7:11.
As a relational arousal-dynamic: the provocation mechanism by which another's action stirs anger within the person — Jer 11:17 (idolatry provoking God to anger).
As identity-level exclusive claim: jealousy as a constitutional attribute that fires with protective passion when its claim is violated — Exo 34:14; Eze 36:5.

Eight distinct operational modes are evidenced across the cluster: judicial verdict, covenant discipline, action-driving impulse, possessing force, restrained-but-present state, sustained moral stance, arousal-dynamic, and identity-level exclusive claim.

The corpus reveals five distinct modes. (1) Receptive-passive mode: grief arrives as an overwhelming inner condition from outside — anguish seizes the person (Jer 49:24 — M03-D-VCG-04), mourning falls upon the city (Isa 29:2 — M03-B-VCG-03), distress finds the psalmist (Psa 119:143 — M03-D-VCG-01). (2) Expressive-outward mode: grief overflows from the inner being into tears (M03-A), groaning (M03-E), and structured mourning acts (M03-B). (3) Generative mode: grief produces inner-being change — repentance (2Cor 7:9 — M03-C-VCG-02), prayer (Psa 18:6 — M03-D-VCG-01), zeal (2Cor 7:11), and moral reformation. (4) Sustained-condition mode: grief settles as a persistent inner weight that drains vitality over time — sorrow spending the psalmist's life (Psa 31:10 — M03-C-VCG-01); pain as a constant inward presence (Psa 38:17 — M03-F-VCG-01). (5) Social-ritual mode: grief takes organised communal form — mourning rites (M03-B-VCG-01), communal lamentation (M03-B-VCG-02), the house of mourning as a shared social space (Jer 16:5 — M03-B-VCG-03).

**[CHAR-1]** E — Four distinct modes appear in the evidence: (1) **spontaneous response** — Jethro's rejoicing (Exo 18:9, cha.dah) on hearing of God's acts is an immediate inner response to external information; the king's exceeding gladness at Daniel's safety (Dan 6:23, te.ev) is a direct relief-and-delight response; (2) **volitional act** — Hab 3:18 ("yet I will rejoice") and Psa 118:24 ("let us rejoice") are deliberate inner choices made independent of circumstances; (3) **sustained orientation** — Psa 89:16 ("who exult in your name all the day") names a perpetual orientation rather than a punctual act; (4) **commanded cultivation** — Psa 2:11; 32:11; Isa 65:18; Zec 9:9 are commands that presuppose the inner state can be directed and sustained by will and formation.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Five distinct modes: (1) **Spontaneous responsive joy** — Aaron's heart-gladness at seeing Moses (Exo 4:14); the people of Beth-shemesh at seeing the ark (1Sa 6:13); the disciples at seeing the risen Lord (Joh 20:20) — immediate inner response triggered by a direct encounter; (2) **Commanded and cultivated joy** — Deuteronomic feast-joy; "Rejoice in the Lord always" (Phili 4:4); "Count it all joy" (Jas 1:2) — joy directed and sustained by volitional practice; (3) **Spirit-produced joy** — "filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit" (Act 13:52); "joy of the Holy Spirit" (1Th 1:6); joy as the Spirit's fruit (Gal 5:22) — joy as a directly Spirit-imparted inner state; (4) **Paradoxical suffering-joy** — "sorrowful, yet always rejoicing" (2Cor 6:10); joy in affliction (2Cor 8:2); co-rejoicing in Paul's imprisonment (Phili 2:17–18) — joy co-existing with and transcending suffering; (5) **Relational co-joy** — sunchairo throughout M04-D; Paul's joy over specific communities (1Th 2:19–20; 3Jo 4) — joy produced by and existing in the bonds between persons.

Love's definition resolves to a structured family of inner-being orientations sharing one mechanism — directed attachment toward an object — whose moral character is entirely determined by the object chosen. Within this shared mechanism, the vocabulary distinguishes three structural registers: love as disposition (the stable inner orientation — chesed, agapē as character), love as act (the commanded and exercised expression — agapaō, enemy-love), and love as condition (the identity-constituting state of being-loved — agapētos). These are not three separate loves but three aspects of love's single operation: the person has a deep stable orientation (disposition), exercises it in specific acts (act), and exists within the love-relationship as constituted by it (condition). The vocabulary arc runs from the ontologically highest (God is love — 1Jo 4:8) through the morally normative (chesed, commanded agapē) to the affective-natural (phileō, dod) to the morally inverted (love of darkness, love of self). No other characteristic in the programme commands a comparable vocabulary range. The definition's boundary with adjacent characteristics (compassion, mercy, kindness) is partially drawn: love is the broader orientation; compassion is love's suffering-triggered mode; mercy and kindness are love's formal relational expressions. The boundaries require Session D precision.

T1 identifies the enabling conditions for mercy-reception (guilt-awareness, humility, persistence, soul-affliction) and T3 maps mercy's faculty engagements. T1 as a whole reveals that contrition is a definitionally complex inner-being condition whose structure is determined by its origin (passive, produced by encounter), its constitutional location (spirit and heart), and its directional logic (downward into brokenness, then threshold toward divine response). The definition tier (T1) establishes that contrition operates in three modes along different relational axes; the relational interface tier (T4) maps those axes to specific directional relationships. The definition tier (T1) positions contrition as a threshold event (not an end-state but a passage toward divine response); the formative tier (T5) confirms and extends this by showing that contrition's productive function is precisely its threshold character — it is the recurring event through which the person is returned to receptivity. T1 reveals that kindness is a structurally composite, other-oriented disposition — not a simple quality. Its essential character is loyal goodwill (chesed = faithfulness + kindness in a single concept), constituted internally by faithfulness, justice, compassion, and forgiveness. It operates in three distinct modes — dispositional orientation, deliberate volitional act, and Spirit-produced formation — and these are not alternatives but layers of a single integrated phenomenon. The immediate and sustained effects are distinct in kind: the immediate response to received kindness is receptive and affective (praise, relief, petition); the sustained effect is formative and dispositional (the person becomes the chasid — one whose character is shaped by chesed over time). The structural opposite is the self-enclosed inward orientation; the counterfeit (chrēstologia) is not merely an absence but an active imposture. T1's most significant intra-tier finding: kindness is primarily dispositional, but the disposition is itself composite — removing any one of its constituent elements (faithfulness, compassion, justice) changes what remains into something that is no longer fully kindness.

The data shows a rich cognate field. Hebrew near-synonyms functioning alongside shalom: (1) Nuach/menuchah (rest, resting-place) — the cessation-dimension of peace; (2) Nachat (H5183A — quietness) — the inner stillness dimension, co-occurs with shaqat in Isa 30:15 at the analytical summit; (3) Shaqat (H8252 — quiet/quieted) — the active quieting, most prominent in its paired form "quietness and trust" (Isa 30:15); (4) Sha'anan (H7600 — at ease) — the ease dimension, positively (Isa 32:18) and negatively (Amo 6:1); (5) Demamah (H1827 — profound silence) — the threshold silence before divine speech. Greek near-synonyms: eirēnē (G1515) is not a synonym but the translation equivalent; hēsuchia/hēsuchios (G2271/G2272) — quietness, the NT equivalent of the Hebrew silence vocabulary (1Pe 3:4 — gentle and quiet spirit); anesis (G0425) — relief/rest from pressure. The cognate field reveals that peace has an inner-face (the silence/stillness vocabulary) and an outer-face (the welfare/wholeness vocabulary), and shalom is the integrative term that spans both.

The data reveals five distinct operational modes (OBS-060-025, OBS-060-051). (1) Performative giving: the act of giving constitutes a covenantal reality — "I will give this land" enacts the covenant (OBS-060-016, OBS-060-036). (2) Responsive giving: giving triggered by the recipient's inner condition — God gives in direct answer to suffering/need (OBS-060-037). (3) Endowing giving: giving that deposits inner-being capacity — Spirit, wisdom, understanding given directly to the inner life (OBS-060-040, OBS-060-041). (4) Judicial giving: giving as moral consequence — giving-over as the expression of inner moral response to faithlessness (OBS-060-042, OBS-060-043). (5) Transformative giving: giving that reverses inner-being states — replacing depletion with fullness, mourning with gladness (OBS-060-048, OBS-060-049, OBS-060-050). In the human direction, a sixth mode is also present: (6) Relinquishing giving: releasing what was received, recognising divine sovereignty over all given goods (OBS-060-044).

T1 as a whole reveals that faithfulness in this registry is structurally composite and directional. The name ("faithfulness") promises a character quality; the OWNER term (na.tan) delivers an action. These are not contradictory — they are complementary aspects of the same inner-being reality: the dispositional quality only becomes faithfulness when it enacts itself (Q&A-016, Q&A-018). The triadic architecture (inner-being source → act → object given) is the definitional shape of this characteristic: it cannot be reduced to disposition alone or act alone (Q&A-017). The five operational modes (Q&A-022) show that this single definitional structure produces radically different expressions depending on what is given and from what inner state — the characteristic is definitionally unified but expressionally plural. The primary dimension (Moral Character) grounds this — it is the character quality that makes the giving faithful rather than merely generous. The definition's most distinctive feature is its disposition-in-action structure: faithfulness is a verb that must be enacted to be real, not a noun that can be possessed without expression.

The disposition-in-action definition (T1) requires the full inner faculty set to be operational (T3). The triadic architecture (source → act → object) maps directly onto faculty engagement: the source requires affect (compassion/anger motivating), volition (choosing to give), and moral evaluation (assessing rightness); the act requires agency (initiating the transfer); the object requires relational capacity (attending to the other's condition). No individual faculty is the characteristic — but the characteristic integrates all of them in a coordinated whole. What this pair reveals: the definition of faithfulness-as-giving is not an abstract proposition but a faculty-integration event. The characteristic exists only when the full inner-being architecture — affective, volitional, agentive, relational — is engaged together. This is why the apex instance (Job 1:21, Isa 50:6) represents the highest form: all faculties operating in unified inner-being act.
